title: Precision vs Throughput — Regional Sizing Workbook (working)
body:
Purpose:
This working workbook captures our current thinking on how quantization and batch sizing affect regional GPU fleet sizing. Focus is on practical heuristics teams can use to estimate required GPUs by region for a multi-model hosted offering while bounding customer-visible quality regressions.

Scope:
- Models: mid-to-large size LLMs (7B — 70B family variants) we serve today.
- Quantization candidates: FP16 (baseline), INT8 simulated (post-training quant), 4-bit (Q4_0, Q4_1), 3-bit experiments.
- Batch strategies: dynamic micro-batching (up to 32), continuous batching queues, request-priority lanes (latency SLOs).
- Regions: us-east1, us-west1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1.

High-level takeaway (one-paragraph):
Switching from FP16 to an aggressive Q4 profile reduces per-GPU token cost by ~1.7–2.2x on H100-like hardware at our sequence/shape distribution, enabling fleet reductions of ~35–50% for throughput-dominated workloads. However, for high-quality chat (few-shot, system prompt sensitive), we observed a median quality delta of 0.8–2.4 percentage points on our core evaluation set depending on model size; so we should only apply aggressive quant to non-critical routing tiers or behind quality-monitoring canaries. Batch size increases give linear throughput gains up to the model/hardware limit but increase tail latency; recommended hybrid: small low-latency lanes + larger background batches.

Assumptions (experiment context):
- Baseline input shape: average request = 120 input tokens, 60 generated tokens.
- Mix: 65% single-turn generation, 25% short-chat (<=3 turns), 10% long streams.
- Hardware: H100 (80GB) used as primary baseline; A100 80GB present in older pools. For conservative sizing assume H100 throughput = 1.0x.
- SLO targets: p95 latency < 450ms for low-latency lane; background lane p95 < 1.2s acceptable.

Micro-bench summary (representative numbers from internal bench):
| Profile | Relative token/s per GPU (H100 baseline=1.0) | Estimated quality delta vs FP16 (composite eval) | Notes |
| FP16 | 1.00 | 0.0% | Baseline — highest quality
| INT8 | 1.45 | -0.3% | Good win for smaller models after calibration
| Q4_0 | 1.85 | -0.9% | Common sweet spot for throughput
| Q4_1 | 2.05 | -1.3% | Slightly faster, more aggressive rounding
| Q3 (experimental) | 2.6 | -2.0 to -3.5% | Use only for non-critical backfills

Per-GPU sample throughput by model band (tokens/s) *approx*:
- 7B: FP16 4200 t/s, Q4_0 7500 t/s, Q4_1 8700 t/s
- 13B: FP16 2400 t/s, Q4_0 4300 t/s, Q4_1 5000 t/s
- 34–70B: FP16 700–1100 t/s, Q4_0 1300–2000 t/s
(These numbers derived from continuous-batch benchmarks with typical prefix reuse patterns.)

Sizing formula (simple):
Required GPUs = ceil((peak_tokens_per_sec / per_gpu_tokens_per_sec) * safety_factor)
Where safety_factor = 1.25 for autoscale headroom + 1.05 regional buffer → combine to ~1.3.
Example: us-east peak user-facing tokens/s = 1.2M t/s for a 13B workload, using Q4_0 per-GPU = 4300 t/s → base GPUs = 1,200,000 / 4,300 = 279 → with safety_factor 1.3 → 363 GPUs.

Region-level notes and recommendations:
- us-east1: highest peak. Recommend dedicated low-latency lane sized at FP16 (10% of traffic) + bulk Q4_0 pool for background/burst (remaining 90%). This keeps p95 for interactive flows stable while maximizing cost savings.
- us-west1: traffic ~40% of us-east. Use mixed pool with preference to Q4_1 for non-critical routes. Maintain 12% spare capacity for fast failover.
- eu-west1: lower throughput but stricter quality requirements for some customers. Default to INT8 where validated, hold Q4_0 behind canary gating per-customer opt-in.
- ap-southeast1: avoid aggressive Q3; prefer FP16/INT8, much higher variance due to shorter tails on regional infra.

Latency vs batch tradeoff guidance:
- Small batch (1–4): best p50/p90 latency; p95 grows with concurrency spikes but acceptable for interactive SLOs.
- Medium batch (8–16): best compromise for throughput + stable p95 in steady-state.
- Large batch (24–32): highest tokens/s but p95 often > SLO; use for non-SLO workloads or background processing.
Recommendation: Always provide a priority queue: lane A (batch<=4) for p95 < 450ms, lane B (batch<=16) for normal traffic, lane C (batch<=32) for low-cost bulk jobs. Autoscaler should allow cross-lane spillover under capacity pressure with explicit fallback to higher-latency policies.

Quality monitoring and rollout controls:
- Maintain prompt-level eval sets per customer and model-band. After any quant/batching change, run regression test: if composite quality_delta > 1.5% for a customer eval set -> auto-block full rollout.
- Canary plan: 1% traffic → 5% → 20% → 50% → 100% with 24h observation windows. Key metrics: fidelity_score (composite), cost_per_token, p95 latency, error rate.

Cost impact (illustrative):
- Moving a 13B fleet from FP16 -> Q4_0: estimated infra cost reduction ~38% (compute-dominated).
- Tradeoff is quality risk: for high-volume non-chat generation features this is a net win; for chat or instruction-following prod features prefer a conservative tiering.

Open questions / experiments to run:
1) Run customer-specific evals for 10 highest-revenue customers under Q4_1 for 48h production canary (JIRA-ENG-4592).
2) Measure tail-latency impact of cross-lane spillover with 30% burst events (simulate in canary env).
3) Formalize ‘fidelity_score’ stiching across perplexity/qa/semantic-sim — draft metric in confluence page linked above.

Action items (next 2 weeks):
- Ethan: schedule regional canaries for us-east/us-west with 1% traffic split (by 2026-03-16).
- Sofia: produce per-customer eval bundles for top-10 accounts (due 2026-03-17).
- Priya: update autoscaler config proposal to include lane-based spillover rules (PR referenced above).

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: silent quality regressions for edge-case prompts. Mitigation: increase eval coverage, post-deploy synthetic probing of critical flows.
- Risk: capacity underestimation during bursty events. Mitigation: keep 12–25% reserved GPUs per region and enable cross-region overflow routing.

Notes to reviewers: this is a working workbook — numbers are rough and intended to facilitate sizing conversations with product and sales. Please add row-level comments with model-specific observations or past incidents that should change the safety factors.
